title: From documents to data
paras: From documents to data — that's where this starts. A site appraisal used to be a stack of paper: the development plan and its proposals map, a flood map ordered by post, the heritage list, a drive out to walk the site. Now it's assembling and interrogating datasets. When the evidence is data, your first move is to stack the layers and ask what they say together, querying in parallel instead of reading in sequence. The precise sources and licence references are in the written guide, so I'll stay on the ideas.

Take a field on the edge of a village. You pull its constraints as data over a base map and aerial imagery, then interrogate it: is any part in the Green Belt, a conservation area or its setting, flood zone 2 or 3, a protected wildlife-site impact zone, on or beside ancient woodland, over a former coalfield, in a nutrient catchment? What's the planning history, and what does the plan allocate? By hand that took days; now it's an hour — and the judgement that follows depends entirely on whether each layer was complete, current and lawfully usable. That caveat is the whole subject.

title: The datasets a planner combines
paras: So — the datasets you combine. Designations first: mostly national, mostly open. Heritage is the strongest case. The National Heritage List for England — listed buildings, scheduled monuments, registered parks and gardens, battlefields, protected wrecks, World Heritage Sites — is a single national dataset from Historic England, served through an API, and reliable. Conservation areas are the exception: supplied up from local authorities, so coverage is good but not complete, and boundaries can lag the authority's own. The nature and landscape designations — Green Belt, National Landscapes, the old Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty, National Parks, SSSIs, Special Areas of Conservation, Special Protection Areas, Ramsar sites, ancient woodland, priority habitats — are national and openly viewable, most easily through MAGIC, under the Open Government Licence. The patchy ones are locally held: tree preservation orders and article 4 directions sit with each authority, inconsistently mapped, nowhere near a clean national set.

The physical layers are strong too. The Environment Agency publishes the flood map — zones 2 and 3 — and its risk-of-flooding data openly, and the national LiDAR programme gives whole-England terrain at one metre, useful for levels, earthworks and drainage; just attribute the Agency. The one to watch is agricultural land classification: the provisional version is national but coarse and old, the reliable detailed surveys patchy. So a best-and-most-versatile screen off the provisional map is a first indication, not an answer.

Then two licensing traps, where 'the data exists' collides with 'I can actually use it'. Land Registry's price paid data — sale prices back to the mid-nineties — is open, and boundaries are half-open: the INSPIRE index polygons show freehold registered title extents in England and Wales, free to reuse and republish with attribution, refreshed monthly, but with no owner names. To learn who owns a parcel you buy the title register, a few pounds each, or use the commercial bulk services — and that ownership data carries restrictions on combining and republishing. So boundaries free, owners paid, constrained on reuse. Second, the base map: Ordnance Survey mapping is licensed, not open. Public bodies reach it through the Public Sector Geospatial Agreement, which runs to 2030, and a consultant to a public authority can use it under a contractor licence tied to the job — but a private practice can't lawfully republish it in a report, submission or website without its own paid licence. Hence the licence number in the corner of every professional site plan; get it wrong and the exposure is legal, not just technical.

Then history, policy and imagery — improving but fragmented. Application data lives on each authority's portal, increasingly flowing to the national platform, but there's no complete standardised national set yet; coverage is partial, formats vary. Allocations are moving toward data through the digital-plans work, but most adopted plans are still a PDF with a map, so boundaries get read rather than queried. Aerial and satellite imagery, including historic imagery and change detection, is a real, underused resource for enforcement and monitoring; some open, much licensed, so check terms before you publish a frame. Utilities and infrastructure records are the weakest layer, held by the statutory undertakers, largely not open, obtained by enquiry. And the historic environment record, the definitive account of non-designated archaeology, is local, not national: signpost to it, don't pretend a national layer exists.

title: Interoperability, APIs and machine-readable planning
paras: Interoperability is where the future lies, and it depends less on any single dataset than on datasets talking to each other. Three things make that possible: common data standards, so a flood zone or a listed building means the same everywhere; common identifiers, so a site, a plan and a permission can be joined; and APIs, letting one system query another's data directly instead of a person downloading a file. The shift underneath is from human-read PDFs to machine-read data — when a plan is data, a computer can check a site against it; when it's a PDF, only a person can.

England has taken the first step. Under recent legislation the government laid the first mandatory planning data standards this year — starting with plan timetables and housing-requirement data, applications and decisions to follow — with a check-and-provide service and the national planning data platform. Its honest state matters: a beta, collecting local authority data under draft standards, openly licensed, saying of itself that it doesn't yet cover all of England. The plumbing is mature — the open geospatial viewing and download standards, and the metadata services the older European regime left behind, now giving way to simpler open APIs. What blocks the vision isn't the pipes, it's the content: inconsistent legacy formats, real gaps, licensing, the labour of standardising decades of paper. The standards have started; completeness is years away.

title: Spatial analysis for site assessment
paras: Spatial analysis for site assessment. Once the layers are assembled, this turns them into planning answers. Constraint screening asks the blunt question — does anything designated or hazardous touch this site? — in seconds, not a morning of map-checking. Sieve mapping and site selection, the backbone of a call-for-sites exercise or a land availability assessment, rules out the absolutely constrained and ranks the rest against a consistent set of layers, so you compare like with like. Buffering and proximity answers the 'within' questions — within the setting of a listed building, a wildlife-site impact zone, walking distance of a school or station. And viewshed and terrain, run over the LiDAR, show what a site can see and be seen from, and read slope and levels for drainage and design.

The value is rigour and speed applied to judgement, not a substitute for it. A sieve map doesn't decide which site is right; it makes the trade-offs visible and defensible, so your reasoning starts from a sound, comparable base rather than whichever site was surveyed first — the difference between an assertion and a demonstrated conclusion, which is exactly what counts when a plan is examined or a refusal appealed.

title: Spatial intelligence — the convergence
paras: Spatial intelligence — the convergence. Follow the direction of travel and it arrives at one idea: systems that don't just display map layers but understand how they interact. The destination — spatial intelligence — is selecting a site and getting an evidence-based first-pass assessment assembled automatically: planning history, designations, flood risk, ecology, heritage, access, utilities, demographics, comparable schemes. It's where digital planning, artificial intelligence and geospatial data converge, and where the day of hand-assembly collapses into minutes.

Two disciplines travel with it. First, it compresses the time gathering evidence, not the judgement applied to it — a first-pass assessment is a faster, fuller starting point, not a decision, and every layer still carries its currency, quality and licensing questions. Second, it's an industry direction and a concept, not a product. No platform delivers it today; several will claim to, and I'd endorse none — including PlanRef itself. Naming the convergence just lets you recognise the same pattern behind a dozen competing tools, and judge each on whether its data is actually complete, current and licensed for the use in hand.

title: The hard realities
paras: Now the hard realities — the heart of the subject, not the small print. Fragmentation first: the data sits with different bodies, in different formats, with different gaps, and no single front door — the heritage list, MAGIC, the Environment Agency's services, the Land Registry and each authority's portal are separate worlds you must know your way around.

Currency is the quiet killer. Data ages, and a confident answer on a stale layer is a confident error. Flood mapping is revised, designations added and amended, application data lags — a constraints print from last year may be wrong today, so check the date of the layer, not just the output. Then quality and provenance: know the source and its limits. The provisional agricultural land classification is not a surveyed one; a local conservation-area boundary is only as good as that authority's data; a generalised findspot is not a grid reference. Treating an indicative layer as a precise one is how good tools produce bad advice.

And licensing — the one that bites in law, not accuracy. Much of the most useful data, Ordnance Survey mapping and Land Registry ownership above all, is licensed, and can't be freely combined, published or handed to a client without permission. An integrated tool makes everything look equally available. It isn't. 'The data exists' is not 'I can lawfully use it, and trust it, for this purpose' — and that gap is where professional embarrassment and legal exposure live.

title: What it means for the planner
paras: So what does this mean for the planner? The skill rising in value is data literacy — knowing which dataset answers which question, where it comes from, how current it is, and whether its licence permits what you're about to do. That's now as much part of competent site work as reading a policy or judging a street scene, and it's a genuine advantage: interrogate data well and you produce faster, better-evidenced, more defensible work than someone who can't.

The posture is the one we've argued throughout — an assembled dataset is evidence to be judged, not an answer to be trusted. Check currency and licence, understand provenance, treat the layers as material for judgement rather than the judgement itself, and you get the speed without the errors or the licence liabilities. Trust the picture because it looks complete and you inherit every gap, stale field and restricted layer in it. Data serves the judgement; it doesn't replace it, and the accountability stays where it always was.

title: Practice points
paras: Let me draw this together. Site appraisal is now data assembly, not reading PDFs in sequence — and always separate three questions: can I get the data, is it current, and does its licence permit what I intend, whether combining, publishing, or handing it to a client. 'The data exists' is not 'I can use it'.

On licensing: Ordnance Survey mapping is licensed — public bodies use it under the Public Sector Geospatial Agreement to 2030, private practices need a paid licence to republish base mapping, hence the licence number on every site plan. Land Registry is boundaries free, owners paid: the price paid data and INSPIRE polygons are open but carry no owner names, and ownership comes from charged, reuse-restricted title data.

On reliability: the National Heritage List is the strong national layer, an open API-served dataset; conservation areas are patchier, supplied by local authorities. MAGIC covers the nature and countryside designations, all openly viewable. LiDAR is national and open at one metre — attribute the Environment Agency. And keep the provisional agricultural land classification indicative, not conclusive; the detailed surveys are patchy.

On the gaps: the national planning data platform is a real beta that doesn't yet cover all of England; the first mandatory data standards arrived this year, covering timetables and housing requirements, with applications and decisions to follow. Check the date of the layer — currency is a defence. The historic environment record is local, not national. Utilities data is obtained by enquiry, not downloaded. Spatial intelligence is a concept, not a purchase. And finally: judge the data, don't trust the picture — interrogate it well and you gain an advantage, trust it blindly and you inherit its errors.

title: Sources
paras: A last word on sources. The full list — the platform's status pages, the government's data-standards announcement, the Ordnance Survey and Land Registry licensing pages, the Environment Agency, Natural England and Defra services, the Historic England heritage list, and the geospatial standards — is in the written guide, with the links.

The one thing to carry from it: this was written for England and the UK as things stand now, and coverage, currency and licence terms all move. So before you rely on a layer, combine it, or republish it on a live matter, re-check the provider's licence and how complete that national dataset really is.
